claim: 26 PD patients were tested ON and OFF dopaminergic medication
source: We tested 26 PD patients ON and OFF dopaminergic medication (PD ON and PD OFF) and 29 healthy age-matched controls (HC) on a rewarded eye-movement task that separated effects of contingent and non-contingent motivation (see Figure 1a for task, see Table 1 for participant details).
evidence: Stated directly in the manuscript text describing the study participants

claim: 29 healthy age-matched controls were tested
source: We tested 26 PD patients ON and OFF dopaminergic medication (PD ON and PD OFF) and 29 healthy age-matched controls (HC) on a rewarded eye-movement task that separated effects of contingent and non-contingent motivation (see Figure 1a for task, see Table 1 for participant details).
evidence: Stated directly in the manuscript text describing the study participants

claim: When PD patients were ON dopamine, they had greater response vigour (peak saccadic velocity residuals) for contingent rewards
source: When PD patients were ON dopamine, they had greater response vigour (peak saccadic velocity residuals) for contingent rewards, whereas when PD patients were OFF medication, they had greater vigour for guaranteed rewards.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental finding in the abstract

claim: When PD patients were OFF medication, they had greater vigour for guaranteed rewards
source: When PD patients were ON dopamine, they had greater response vigour (peak saccadic velocity residuals) for contingent rewards, whereas when PD patients were OFF medication, they had greater vigour for guaranteed rewards.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental finding in the abstract

claim: Dopaminergic medication significantly modulated how contingent and guaranteed motivation affected motor vigour (three-way interaction on peak velocity residuals, p=0.0023)
source: Dopaminergic medication significantly modulated how contingent and guaranteed motivation affected motor vigour (Figure 2a, three-way interaction on peak velocity residuals, p=0.0023; see Table 2 for statistics).
evidence: Statistical test result with p-value and reference to Figure 2a

claim: When ON medication, patients were motivated by contingency but not reward expectation (contingency*motivation, p=0.0170)
source: This was because, when ON medication, patients were motivated by contingency but not reward expectation (separate two-way ANOVA in PD ON: contingency*motivation, p=0.0170; see Supplementary file 1A)
evidence: Statistical test result from two-way ANOVA

claim: After overnight withdrawal of medication there was a borderline significant interaction in the opposite direction (PD OFF ANOVA: p=0.0501)
source: whereas after overnight withdrawal of medication there was a borderline significant interaction in the opposite direction, as PD OFF were motivated by reward expectation but not contingency (PD OFF ANOVA: p=0.0501; Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: Statistical test result from ANOVA

claim: PD patients had slower saccadic RTs, and slower, smaller and more variable saccades compared to age-matched controls
source: PD patients had slower saccadic RTs, and slower, smaller and more variable saccades compared to age-matched controls.
evidence: Direct comparison between PD patients and controls

claim: HC were similar to PD ON dopamine
source: (b) HC were similar to PD ON dopamine (please note the different y-axis limits).
evidence: Figure 2b caption describing similarity between groups

claim: Saccadic RT had an effect of contingency as saccades started faster for Performance and Random conditions than 10 p or 0 p conditions (p=0.0396)
source: Saccadic RT had an effect of contingency as saccades started faster for Performance and Random conditions than 10 p or 0 p conditions (Figure 2d, p=0.0396).
evidence: Statistical test result with reference to Figure 2d

claim: Endpoint variability had a contingency*motivation interaction (p=0.0482) as variability was higher for 0 p condition
source: Endpoint variability had a contingency*motivation interaction (Figure 2e, p=0.0482) as variability was higher for 0 p condition.
evidence: Statistical test result with reference to Figure 2e

claim: Raw peak velocity had an effect of motivation, as both types of motivation increased speed (p=0.0110)
source: Raw peak velocity had an effect of motivation, as both types of motivation increased speed (Figure 2f, p=0.0110)
evidence: Statistical test result with reference to Figure 2f

claim: HC peak velocity residuals were not affected by contingency, motivation or the interaction (p>0.05)
source: The HC peak velocity residuals were not affected by contingency, motivation or the interaction (p>0.05; see Table 3)
evidence: Statistical test results for healthy controls

claim: Guaranteed rewards (10 p – 0 p) lead to greater velocity early in the saccade for PD OFF (p<0.05)
source: However, guaranteed rewards (10 p – 0 p) lead to greater velocity early in the saccade for PD OFF (p<0.05; Figure 3c), which was significantly different from PD ON (p<0.05).
evidence: Cluster-wise permutation test result with reference to Figure 3c

claim: Acceleration traces showed PD OFF had greater acceleration early in the movement for guaranteed rewards (p<0.05)
source: Acceleration traces showed this was due to PD OFF having greater acceleration early in the movement (Figure 3d, p<0.05).
evidence: Cluster-wise permutation test result with reference to Figure 3d

claim: HC showed no effects of contingent or guaranteed rewards on velocity or acceleration
source: HC showed no effects of contingent or guaranteed rewards on velocity or acceleration, perhaps unsurprising as there were no differences in overall velocity as reported above.
evidence: Statement of null findings in healthy controls

claim: Permutation testing revealed no differences between HC and PD ON or OFF for velocity or acceleration (p>0.05)
source: Permutation testing revealed no differences between HC and PD ON or OFF for velocity or acceleration (p>0.05).
evidence: Statistical test result from permutation testing

claim: Guaranteed rewards led to greater autocorrelation early in the saccades for PD OFF than ON
source: In the current study, guaranteed rewards led to greater autocorrelation early in the saccades for PD OFF than ON (Figure 4e & g).
evidence: Statement of finding with reference to Figure 4

claim: No correlation was found between effects of contingent and guaranteed rewards on peak saccade velocity residuals in PD ON, PD OFF or HC separately (p>0.05)
source: We found no correlation between effects of contingent and guaranteed rewards on peak saccade velocity residuals in PD ON, PD OFF or HC separately, nor a correlation between medication states, nor between the drug-induced changes in the effects (p>0.05; see Figure 5 legend for statistics).
evidence: Statistical test results for correlations

claim: There were no significant effects or interactions of dopamine and reward on pupil responses (p>0.05)
source: There were no significant effects or interactions (p>0.05; Figure 6, see Supplementary file 2A-C for statistics), suggesting that dopamine and reward did not affect pupil responses in PD patients.
evidence: Statistical test results with reference to Figure 6

claim: No correlations were found between UPDRS-III scores and reward effects on peak velocity residuals in PD ON or OFF
source: We found no correlations between UPDRS-III scores and reward effects on peak velocity residuals in PD ON (Guaranteed: ρ = −0.1256, p=0.5410; Contingent: ρ = −0.2327, p=0.2527) or OFF (Guaranteed: ρ = −0.2067, p=0.3110; Contingent: ρ = 0.1553, p=0.4487).
evidence: Correlation statistics with p-values

claim: No significant correlations were found between apathy/depression questionnaires and contingent or guaranteed motivational effects on peak velocity residuals in PD ON or OFF (p>0.05)
source: We found no significant correlations between these questionnaires and contingent or guaranteed motivational effects on peak velocity residuals in PD ON or OFF (p>0.05, see Supplementary file 4 for statistics).
evidence: Statistical test results for questionnaire correlations

claim: No significant clusters of frequencies where patients differed in ocular tremor were found (p>0.05)
source: To quantify ocular tremor, we performed Fourier transforms on the eye position in the early (200–700 ms) and late (700–1200 ms) fixation periods, and compared these between conditions with cluster-wise permutation tests to look for clusters of frequencies where patients differed. We found no significant clusters (p>0.05).
evidence: Statistical test result from cluster-wise permutation tests

claim: Organisms expend more effort when their actions can lead to rewards, as the value of the reward offsets the extra effort expended to attain them
source: Organisms expend more effort when their actions can lead to rewards, as the value of the reward offsets the extra effort expended to attain them (Kool and Botvinick, 2018; Manohar et al., 2015; Niv et al., 2006; Shenhav et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: Organisms will expend extra effort even if the extra effort does not increase the reward they receive
source: They will even do so if the extra effort does not increase the reward they receive (Glaser et al., 2016; Milstein and Dorris, 2007; Xu-Wilson et al., 2009), indicating that mere expectation of reward is enough to justify the effort cost.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Mere expectation of reward is enough to justify the effort cost
source: They will even do so if the extra effort does not increase the reward they receive (Glaser et al., 2016; Milstein and Dorris, 2007; Xu-Wilson et al., 2009), indicating that mere expectation of reward is enough to justify the effort cost.
evidence: Inference drawn from cited research findings

claim: Motivation allows actions to be directed towards goals and energises actions when rewards are expected
source: Motivation, which promotes this effort expenditure, has two facets: it allows actions to be directed towards goals, and it energises our actions when rewards are expected (Niv et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: The two aspects of motivation (goal-directed and energising) are not always coupled
source: These two aspects are not always coupled. For example, employees might be salaried, where a fixed reward is guaranteed irrespective of achievements, or they might receive merit-based pay that is contingent on meeting performance targets (Lazear, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation and example

claim: Contingent rewards motivate us because we understand the causal relation between successful actions and reward
source: Contingent rewards motivate us because we understand the causal relation between successful actions and reward. This is instrumental, in that we apply knowledge of action-outcome associations.
evidence: Theoretical explanation based on established concepts

claim: Dopaminergic input to dorsal striatum is necessary for instrumental motivation in animals
source: In animals, dopaminergic input to dorsal striatum is necessary for instrumental motivation (Lex and Hauber, 2010b).
evidence: Supported by citation to animal research

claim: Tonic dopamine encodes expected reward rate, such that in a rich environment agents are motivated to respond faster to maximise the rewards they receive
source: One proposed mechanism for this is that tonic dopamine encodes expected reward rate, such that in a rich environment agents are motivated to respond faster to maximise the rewards they receive (Niv et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to theoretical work

claim: Dopamine can be viewed as signalling an opportunity cost– time is more costly when reward is available, and so organisms act faster
source: Equally, dopamine can be viewed as signalling an opportunity cost– time is more costly when reward is available, and so organisms act faster (Otto and Daw, 2019; Shadmehr et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical work

claim: Pavlovian-to-Instrumental transfer requires dopamine projections to nucleus accumbens
source: This phenomenon, known as Pavlovian-to-Instrumental transfer, requires dopamine projections to nucleus accumbens (Hall et al., 2001; Kelley and Delfs, 1991; Talmi et al., 2008; Wassum et al., 2013; Wyvell and Berridge, 2000).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: Autoshaping or sign-tracking relies on nucleus accumbens dopamine
source: Similarly, animals tend to approach stimuli associated with rewards, even in the absence of action-contingency, a behaviour called autoshaping or sign-tracking, which also relies on nucleus accumbens dopamine (Day et al., 2006; Di Ciano et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: The dopaminergic basis of instrumental and Pavlovian motivation could potentially explain the impaired motivation seen in PD patients and the rescue of such deficits by rewards
source: The dopaminergic basis of instrumental and Pavlovian motivation could potentially explain the impaired motivation seen in PD patients and the rescue of such deficits by rewards (Ang et al., 2018; Chong et al., 2015; de Wit et al., 2011; Kojovic et al., 2014).
evidence: Inference supported by citations to PD research

claim: In certain situations, motivation by reward can paradoxically be stronger in patients with low dopamine
source: However in certain situations, motivation by reward can paradoxically be stronger in patients with low dopamine (Aarts et al., 2012; Timmer et al., 2018), making dopamine's exact role in motivation unclear.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Both contingency and expectation can separately motivate behaviour, and these effects are independent rather than correlated or antagonistic
source: However, experimental control of expectation and contingency allows them to be dissociated (Manohar et al., 2017), which reveals that both contingency and expectation can separately motivate behaviour, and that these effects are independent rather than correlated or antagonistic, suggesting distinct mechanisms.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: A saccade's velocity is tightly governed by its amplitude, a relation known as the 'main sequence'
source: A saccade's velocity is tightly governed by its amplitude, a relation known as the 'main sequence' (Bahill et al., 1975).
evidence: Supported by citation to established research

claim: Peak saccade velocity residuals measure how much faster each saccade is than the speed predicted from its amplitude
source: To account for this, we regressed out the effect of amplitude on peak velocity leaving peak saccade velocity residuals as our main measure of response vigour (see Figure 1e), as in previous work (Blundell et al., 2018; Manohar et al., 2017; Muhammed et al., 2020; Muhammed et al., 2016; Van Opstal et al., 1990). This measures how much faster each saccade is than the speed predicted from its amplitude.
evidence: Methodological explanation supported by citations

claim: Positive (negative) residuals mean a particular saccade was faster (slower) than predicted by the main sequence
source: Thus, positive (negative) residuals mean a particular saccade was faster (slower) than predicted by the main sequence, and makes response vigour independent of any changes to saccade amplitude also caused by our manipulations or by group differences between PD patients and HC.
evidence: Methodological explanation

claim: Faster movements are known to be more error-prone
source: Faster movements are known to be more error-prone (Harris and Wolpert, 1998; Harris and Wolpert, 2006), but motivation can attenuate this effect, making movements more accurate (Manohar et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Motivation can attenuate the speed-accuracy tradeoff, making movements more accurate
source: Faster movements are known to be more error-prone (Harris and Wolpert, 1998; Harris and Wolpert, 2006), but motivation can attenuate this effect, making movements more accurate (Manohar et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Autocorrelation of eye position over time within saccades provides an indicator of corrective motor signals during movements
source: Autocorrelation of eye position over time within saccades provides an indicator of corrective motor signals during movements: noise accumulates during movements, so that variability early in a movement causes endpoint error. This is manifest in autocorrelation, where across trials the eye position at early time-points predicts late time-points.
evidence: Methodological explanation based on established principles

claim: Negative feedback signals correct movement errors during the saccade, and manifest as reductions in autocorrelation
source: Negative feedback signals correct movement errors during the saccade, and manifest as reductions in this autocorrelation (Codol et al., 2020; Manohar et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Feedback provided by corrective motor signals can be increased by incentives
source: This feedback, provided by corrective motor signals, can be increased by incentives (Codol et al., 2019; Manohar et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: The two motivational effects were uncorrelated across people and between medication states, indicating that dopamine does not promote one type of motivation over another in a competitive fashion
source: The two motivational effects were uncorrelated across people and between medication states (Figure 5) indicating that dopamine does not promote one type of motivation over another in a competitive fashion, and were not associated with changes in pupil dilatation (Figure 6).
evidence: Inference drawn from statistical analysis results

claim: Reward expectation and contingency provide distinct motivational drives, which can be dissociated by dopaminergic medication
source: Rather, reward expectation and contingency provide distinct motivational drives (Figure 7), which can be dissociated by dopaminergic medication.
evidence: Summary conclusion drawn from experimental findings

claim: Dopamine is necessary for contingent motivation
source: The results suggest that dopamine is necessary for contingent motivation.
evidence: Inference drawn from experimental results

claim: Contingent motivation requires the use of stimulus-action-outcome associations for goal-directed behaviour
source: Contingent motivation requires the use of stimulus-action-outcome associations for goal-directed behaviour (Daw and Dayan, 2014; Dickinson, 1985), while reward expectation can occur via stimulus-outcome associations (Niv et al., 2007) that do not require understanding the causal role of action.
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical work

claim: Reward expectation can occur via stimulus-outcome associations that do not require understanding the causal role of action
source: Contingent motivation requires the use of stimulus-action-outcome associations for goal-directed behaviour (Daw and Dayan, 2014; Dickinson, 1985), while reward expectation can occur via stimulus-outcome associations (Niv et al., 2007) that do not require understanding the causal role of action.
evidence: Supported by citation to theoretical work

claim: Dorsomedial striatum dopaminergic lesions impair action-outcome associations in rodents
source: Our results align with rodent work demonstrating that dorsomedial striatum dopaminergic lesions impair action-outcome associations, such that animals continue to respond to previously rewarding cues even when action-contingency is removed (Lex and Hauber, 2010b).
evidence: Supported by citation to animal research

claim: Dopamine is necessary for behaviours involving a causal state-action-state model, but not simple value-guided actions
source: At a more general level, our result is also consistent with dopamine being necessary for behaviours involving a causal state-action-state model (Sharpe et al., 2017), but not simple value-guided actions (Sharp et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Dopamine might reduce reward expectation effects through a different mechanism than tonic dopamine coupling vigour to average reward rate
source: Our finding reveals that dopaminergic medication attenuates the cue-driven reward expectation effect on vigour can be contrasted with previous work suggesting that tonic dopamine couples vigour to average reward rate (Beierholm et al., 2013; Niv et al., 2007). Our adaptive reward schedule held the average reward rate constant over time, while manipulating the average reward rate within each condition, such that the guaranteed 10 p and 0 p trials had different expected rewards. Dopamine might reduce these expectation effects through a different mechanism
evidence: Inference drawn from comparison with prior research

claim: Slow, tonic dopaminergic activity is not related to Pavlovian-to-Instrumental transfer
source: This aligns with the finding that slow, tonic dopaminergic activity is not related to Pavlovian-to-Instrumental transfer (Wassum et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Fast phasic dopaminergic responses in the nucleus accumbens encode average reward rate, but slow tonic responses do not
source: An additional challenge to the tonic dopamine theory of reward expectation comes from the finding that fast phasic dopaminergic responses in the nucleus accumbens encode average reward rate, but slow tonic responses do not (Mohebi et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Reward expectation signals are independent of ventral tegmental area dopaminergic neuron firing, and may instead be due to 'local' control over nucleus accumbens core dopamine release
source: That study suggests that reward expectation signals are independent of ventral tegmental area dopaminergic neuron firing, and may instead be due to 'local' control over nucleus accumbens core dopamine release.
evidence: Inference drawn from cited research

claim: Dopamine is depleted in PD via dopamine-neuron death in the substantia nigra and ventral tegmental area
source: As dopamine is depleted in PD via dopamine-neuron death in the substantia nigra and ventral tegmental area, local dopamine release in other areas may be relatively preserved, and thus still able to influence vigour when PD patients are without dopamine.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of PD pathology

claim: Local dopamine release in areas other than substantia nigra and ventral tegmental area may be relatively preserved in PD
source: As dopamine is depleted in PD via dopamine-neuron death in the substantia nigra and ventral tegmental area, local dopamine release in other areas may be relatively preserved, and thus still able to influence vigour when PD patients are without dopamine.
evidence: Speculative inference based on PD pathology

claim: The increased noise in the guaranteed reward condition was attenuated via negative feedback
source: However, this noise increase did not persist until the end of the saccade, as there was no increase in autocorrelation at the end of the saccade (Figure 4) and no greater endpoint variability (Figure 2e) – indeed, guaranteed rewards actually decreased endpoint variability, although this was not affected by dopamine. This offers some indirect evidence that the increased noise in this condition was attenuated via negative feedback (c.f. Manohar et al., 2019).
evidence: Inference drawn from data patterns with citation

claim: The lack of either type of motivation in the older HC is surprising given that in healthy young adults, both contingent and guaranteed rewards increase saccade velocity
source: The lack of either type of motivation in the older HC is surprising given that in healthy young adults, both contingent and guaranteed rewards increase saccade velocity (Manohar et al., 2017).
evidence: Comparison with cited prior research

claim: Ageing may decrease both contingent-motivation and reward-expectation
source: This could suggest ageing decreases both contingent-motivation and reward-expectation, although a study directly comparing ages would be needed to conclude this.
evidence: Speculative inference from observed pattern

claim: Both ageing and PD may decrease the influence of rewards on pupil size
source: The motivational effects reported here were not related to any pupillary responses, unlike our previous findings in young people, which may be due to both ageing and PD decreasing the influence of rewards on pupil size (Manohar and Husain, 2015; Muhammed et al., 2016).
evidence: Inference supported by citations to prior research

claim: The nucleus accumbens and ventral pallidum modulate their activity by reward expectation
source: The nucleus accumbens and ventral pallidum modulate their activity by reward expectation (Mohebi et al., 2019; Tachibana and Hikosaka, 2012), while the caudate nucleus is active when rewards are contingent on behaviour (Lex and Hauber, 2010a; Tricomi et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: The caudate nucleus is active when rewards are contingent on behaviour
source: The nucleus accumbens and ventral pallidum modulate their activity by reward expectation (Mohebi et al., 2019; Tachibana and Hikosaka, 2012), while the caudate nucleus is active when rewards are contingent on behaviour (Lex and Hauber, 2010a; Tricomi et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Both the caudate and accumbens/pallidum project to the output nuclei of the basal ganglia, allowing saccade initiation via the superior colliculus
source: Both the caudate and accumbens/pallidum project to the output nuclei of the basal ganglia, allowing saccade initiation via the superior colliculus, which controls not only the direction of saccades, but also their instantaneous velocity during the movement (Smalianchuk et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: The superior colliculus controls not only the direction of saccades, but also their instantaneous velocity during the movement
source: Both the caudate and accumbens/pallidum project to the output nuclei of the basal ganglia, allowing saccade initiation via the superior colliculus, which controls not only the direction of saccades, but also their instantaneous velocity during the movement (Smalianchuk et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Contingent motivation and reward expectation both lead to motivational signals affecting the superior colliculus' activity controlling the velocity and acceleration of saccades, and these are differentially affected by dopamine
source: We propose contingent motivation and reward expectation both lead to motivational signals affecting the superior colliculus' activity controlling the velocity and acceleration of saccades, and these are differentially affected by dopamine (Figure 7), although we remain agnostic as to the mechanism for this difference.
evidence: Theoretical proposal based on experimental findings

claim: Possible mechanisms for dissociative dopamine influence include separate dopaminergic regions innervating the two pathways, 'global' vs 'local' signalling, or different expression of D1-like and D2-like receptors
source: Possibilities include the two systems receiving input from separate regions of the dopaminergic system which are differentially depleted in PD (e.g. dopamine overdose hypothesis [Cools, 2006]), differences in 'global' and 'local' dopamine signals (Mohebi et al., 2019), or differences in D1-like and D2-like receptor expression within these systems (Surmeier et al., 2007; Yetnikoff et al., 2014).
evidence: Speculative possibilities supported by citations

claim: Dopaminergic medication may be a potential treatment for impairments in contingent motivation, but not for deficits related to reward expectation
source: This suggests that dopaminergic medication may be a potential treatment for impairments in contingent motivation, but not for deficits related to reward expectation.
evidence: Clinical implication inferred from experimental findings

claim: Thirty PD patients were recruited from volunteer databases in the University of Oxford
source: Thirty PD patients were recruited from volunteer databases in the University of Oxford.
evidence: Direct statement of recruitment method

claim: All PD patients were taking levodopa medication
source: They were all taking levodopa medication, and some were also taking monoamine oxidase inhibitors and/or dopamine agonists (Table 3).
evidence: Direct statement of medication status

claim: Some PD patients were also taking monoamine oxidase inhibitors and/or dopamine agonists
source: They were all taking levodopa medication, and some were also taking monoamine oxidase inhibitors and/or dopamine agonists (Table 3).
evidence: Direct statement of medication status

claim: PD patients were withdrawn from standard release medication for 16+ hours and controlled-release medication for 24+ hours
source: They were randomly assigned to be tested ON or OFF medication first, and withdrawn from standard release medication for 16+ hours and controlled-release medication for 24+ hours.
evidence: Direct statement of medication withdrawal protocol

claim: Two patients did not complete both sessions, and two did not have enough trials that passed all the criteria so were excluded
source: Two patients did not complete both sessions, and two did not have enough trials that passed all the criteria (see Analysis section) so were excluded, leaving 26 patients.
evidence: Direct statement of exclusions

claim: Thirty healthy controls were recruited from volunteer databases and tested once
source: Thirty healthy controls (HC) were recruited from volunteer databases also, and tested once, and one HC was excluded for insufficient trials passing the criteria.
evidence: Direct statement of recruitment and testing

claim: One HC was excluded for insufficient trials passing the criteria
source: Thirty healthy controls (HC) were recruited from volunteer databases also, and tested once, and one HC was excluded for insufficient trials passing the criteria.
evidence: Direct statement of exclusion

claim: The sample size of 30 participants in each group was chosen based on previous experiments with this task that yielded robust effects
source: We recruited 30 participants in each group as this was the sample size used in previous experiments with this task and yielded robust effects (Manohar et al., 2017).
evidence: Justification for sample size based on prior research

claim: Sensitivity power calculations showed the study would detect effect sizes above 0.46 (α = 0.05, power = 0.8, sample size = 30)
source: Sensitivity power calculations showed this would detect effect sizes above 0.46 (Faul et al., 2009) (α = 0.05, power = 0.8, sample size = 30), although as we only included 26 PD in the analysis, this effect size rose to 0.5.
evidence: Power calculation results

claim: With 26 PD patients in the analysis, the detectable effect size rose to 0.5
source: Sensitivity power calculations showed this would detect effect sizes above 0.46 (Faul et al., 2009) (α = 0.05, power = 0.8, sample size = 30), although as we only included 26 PD in the analysis, this effect size rose to 0.5.
evidence: Power calculation results

claim: Ethical approval was granted by the South Central Oxford A REC (18/SC/0448)
source: All participants gave written informed consent, and ethical approval was granted by the South Central Oxford A REC (18/SC/0448).
evidence: Direct statement of ethical approval

claim: In the Performance condition, rewards were based upon response time
source: Participants could only affect the outcome in the Performance condition (by moving faster); all others were independent of their speed. In the Performance condition, rewards were based upon response time (i.e. total time between the target appearing and gaze arriving at the target), which is only minimally influenced by saccade velocity.
evidence: Direct description of experimental design

claim: Participants were rewarded when response time was quicker than their recent median response time for the last 20 Performance trials, which yielded a 50% reward rate overall
source: Participants were rewarded when response time was quicker than their recent median response time for the last 20 Performance trials, which thus yielded a 50% reward rate overall.
evidence: Direct description of reward contingency

claim: The Random condition acts as a control with a random 50% of trials rewarded, and thus equal expected value but with no performance-contingency
source: The Random condition acts as a control to these trials, with a random 50% of trials rewarded, and thus equal expected value but with no performance-contingency.
evidence: Direct description of control condition

claim: Participants always received feedback on their speed (fast/slow) regardless of reward to control for intrinsic motivation
source: When rewards are contingent, people get feedback about how they performed. This itself is known to increase motivation, independent of reward – a phenomenon termed intrinsic motivation. To control for this, we ensured participants always received feedback on their speed (fast/slow, using median split over 20 previous trials in that condition – i.e. the same criteria as for contingent rewards), regardless of reward.
evidence: Direct description of experimental control

claim: The feedback modalities were counterbalanced: two blocks gave auditory feedback for speed and visual feedback for reward, and vice versa for the other two blocks
source: In order to ensure the speed feedback and reward were matched in physical salience, the feedback modalities were counterbalanced. Two blocks gave auditory feedback for speed and visual feedback for reward, and vice versa for the other two blocks, with order randomised across participants.
evidence: Direct description of experimental design

claim: No effects of modality were found on any of the measures of interest (p>0.05)
source: We also found no effects of modality on any of the measures of interest (p>0.05), so collapsed across the two modalities for all the analyses.
evidence: Statistical test result

claim: There were 12 types of each trial in a block, in a random order, and participants completed four blocks
source: There were 12 types of each trial in a block, in a random order, and participants completed four blocks.
evidence: Direct description of experimental design

claim: Saccades with peak velocities outside 80–2500°s−1 were excluded
source: Saccades with peak velocities outside 80–2500°s−1 were excluded, as were trials where participants reached the target before 180 ms or after 580 ms.
evidence: Direct description of exclusion criteria

claim: Trials where participants reached the target before 180 ms or after 580 ms were excluded
source: Saccades with peak velocities outside 80–2500°s−1 were excluded, as were trials where participants reached the target before 180 ms or after 580 ms.
evidence: Direct description of exclusion criteria

claim: Two PD patients and one HC had fewer than 10 trials that passed the criteria for one condition, so were excluded from the analysis
source: Two PD patients and one HC had fewer than 10 trials that passed these criteria for one condition, so were excluded from the analysis.
evidence: Direct statement of exclusions

claim: The regression of velocity against amplitude was done for each participant's separate session
source: To remove the main sequence effect of amplitude on velocity (Bahill et al., 1975; Harris and Wolpert, 2006), we regressed velocity against amplitude and took the peak velocity residuals as our measure of interest. This measures the difference between the velocity predicted by the main sequence, and the velocity actually recorded, with positive (negative) values meaning faster (slower) velocity. This was done for each participant's separate session.
evidence: Direct description of analysis method

claim: The approach of using velocity residuals has been used before by multiple researchers
source: This approach has been used before, by us and others (Blundell et al., 2018; Manohar et al., 2017; Muhammed et al., 2020; Muhammed et al., 2016; Van Opstal et al., 1990)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Using velocity residuals is similar to simply including amplitude as a covariate when analysing raw peak velocity, but it does not reduce the degrees of freedom and yields simpler to interpret results
source: and it is similar to simply including amplitude as a covariate when analysing raw peak velocity, but it does not reduce the degrees of freedom and yields simpler to interpret results.
evidence: Methodological justification

claim: Since motivation increases amplitude, including amplitude as a covariate would mean that amplitude would compete with motivation to explain variance in velocity, potentially resulting in overestimation of motivation effects
source: Moreover since motivation increases amplitude (Manohar et al., 2019), including amplitude as a covariate would mean that amplitude would compete with motivation to explain variance in velocity, potentially resulting in overestimation of motivation effects.
evidence: Methodological justification supported by citation

claim: The findings did not qualitatively change when using the covariate approach instead of velocity residuals
source: Our findings did not qualitatively change when we used the covariate approach instead.
